column5: teach the divine paths
column6: The commentary treats guidance as both knowing a route and being led along it; the psalm asks God to make his ways known and teach his paths.

column5: lead me in your truth
column6: The commentary's “lead us on the straight path” is a prayer for continuing direction; this verse asks God to lead the speaker in truth and teach him.

column5: teach me your way; unite my heart
column6: The commentary links walking God's way with exclusive worship; this prayer asks to be taught God's way in order to walk in truth with an undivided heart.

column5: good Spirit; level ground
column6: The commentary asks God to guide a dependent traveler and stresses a level, sustained walk; the psalm asks God to teach his will and have his good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground.

column5: level path amid enemies
column6: The commentary hears the straight path as a route that must be followed and protected; the psalm asks God to teach his way and lead the speaker on a level path despite hostile witnesses.

column5: paths of righteousness
column6: The commentary asks for guidance along a lived route; the psalm's shepherd leads the speaker on tracks of righteousness, joining direction with sustained care.

column5: supplication; straight path; brooks
column6: The commentary's collective petition asks God to keep worshipers on the way; Jeremiah pictures a weeping returning people led by God, with supplication, along a straight path to water where they will not stumble.

column5: blind led on an unknown way
column6: The commentary describes people who cannot find the route without a guide; God promises here to lead the blind by a way they do not know, turning darkness to light and rough ground level.

column5: the voice says, “this is the way”
column6: The commentary presents guidance as an ongoing walk rather than a one-time conversion; this verse gives travelers a voice directing them to keep walking the way when they veer right or left.

column5: God makes paths straight
column6: The commentary asks God to lead a community already devoted to him; Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one's ways brings his making the paths straight.

column5: teaches; leads in the way
column6: The commentary makes God the source of guidance and its ongoing teacher; here God says he teaches what is beneficial and leads Israel in the way it should go.

column5: the path of the righteous made level
column6: The commentary connects the straight path with an even, unbent course; Isaiah says the path of the righteous is level because God makes it smooth.

column5: highway of holiness; the redeemed
column6: The commentary identifies the requested route with the company of those favored by God; Isaiah's highway is called the holy way and is reserved for the redeemed returning to Zion.

column5: straight road to an inhabited city
column6: The commentary says the road ends in a home that receives the traveler; after the lost and hungry wanderers cry for help, God leads them by a straight way to a city where they can dwell.

column5: travelers cry to God for help
column6: The commentary connects the request to be guided with the preceding plea for help; this verse depicts travelers crying to God in distress and being delivered before the straight road and city of the next verse.

column5: God leads the redeemed to his holy abode
column6: The commentary's journey ends in a place of welcome; the Song of the Sea says God leads the people he redeemed toward his holy dwelling by steadfast love.

column5: bring and plant at the sanctuary
column6: The commentary hears guidance as arrival at a home or refuge; Moses' song asks God to bring the people to his mountain and plant them at the sanctuary he established.

column5: the Lord goes before Israel
column6: The commentary names Moses and Aaron as people led on the straight way; in the Exodus narrative God goes before Israel as cloud and fire to guide their day-and-night wilderness journey.

column5: God goes ahead to find a camp
column6: The commentary's guide goes in front and shows where to walk; Moses recalls God going ahead of Israel to find camping places and show the route.

column5: the Lord alone guided Israel
column6: The commentary says the request is directed only to the one who can truly guide; Moses' song says the Lord alone led Jacob, with no foreign god beside him.

column5: the ark goes before, seeking a resting place
column6: The commentary's guide goes ahead of the travelers and leads toward a place of rest; the ark precedes Israel in the wilderness to seek a resting place for them.

column5: the guide leads to springs
column6: The commentary connects guidance with reaching a place of shelter and sustaining water; Isaiah says the compassionate guide leads the returning people to springs of water.

column5: continual guidance like a watered garden
column6: The commentary insists that guidance continues along the road and mentions water that sustains life; Isaiah promises that God will guide continually and make the people like a watered garden.

column5: the highways to Zion in the heart
column6: The commentary's path is walked toward a welcomed destination; the pilgrim psalm blesses those whose hearts are set on the highways to God's house.

column5: the valley becomes springs
column6: The commentary associates the road with sustaining water and support for the traveler; this pilgrimage verse describes a dry valley becoming a place of springs on the way to Zion.

column5: from strength to strength, appearing before God
column6: The commentary says the route is a walk that continues until arrival; the pilgrim psalm describes travelers gaining strength as they go until each appears before God in Zion.

column5: make a level path for your feet
column6: The commentary develops uprightness as a bodily walk that must remain straight; Proverbs tells the hearer to make a level path for the feet and have all ways be firm.

column5: do not swerve right or left
column6: The commentary places the straight path between deviations and asks for help to stay on it; Proverbs commands the traveler not to turn right or left but to keep the foot from evil.

column5: ask for the good ancient way and walk in it
column6: The commentary treats guidance as something to be requested repeatedly and then walked; Jeremiah tells the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, though they refuse.

column5: the Lord knows the righteous way; the wicked way perishes
column6: The commentary distinguishes the favored people's path from ways that end in loss; Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous, known by the Lord, with the way of the wicked, which perishes.

column5: choose life rather than death
column6: The commentary names a straight path between opposed outcomes; Moses sets life and death before Israel and calls them to choose life by loving and obeying God.

column5: the Lord's way is justice and righteousness
column6: The commentary says the path is a lived course shaped by worship; God says Abraham's household is to keep the Lord's way by doing righteousness and justice.

column5: limping between two allegiances
column6: The commentary depicts the traveler as wavering and asks for an unwavering path; Elijah challenges Israel for limping between the Lord and Baal and demands a clear choice of whom to serve.

column5: the right way leads to a bride's home
column6: The commentary develops guidance as escorting a bride to the home where she will be received; Abraham's servant says the Lord led him on the right way to find Rebekah as a wife for Isaac.

column5: offerings brought to the chosen place
column6: The commentary's h-d-y word family includes an offering animal brought to its appointed sanctuary; Deuteronomy directs Israel to bring sacrifices and firstborn offerings to the place God chooses.

column5: trust; help; make your ways straight
column6: The commentary presents the request for guidance as trustful dependence on God, not self-direction; Sirach tells the faithful to trust God for help, make their ways straight, and hope in him.

column5: ask God to make your ways straight
column6: The commentary frames guidance as a direct request to God along life's journey; Tobit advises blessing God and asking him to make one's ways and plans straight.

column5: paths set right by divine wisdom
column6: The commentary asks God to lead a community into the right way; Wisdom says that by divine wisdom the paths of people on earth were set right and they learned what pleases God.

column5: Tefillat ha-derekh
column6: The commentary's petition asks God to lead the worshipers along the way; the travelers' prayer asks God to lead and direct the traveler safely on the road.

column5: prayers on entering and leaving a city
column6: The commentary hears guidance as a journey toward a place that will receive the traveler; this passage gives prayers asking God to lead a traveler into and out of a city in peace.

column5: the two spirits and their ways
column6: The commentary places the straight way between the ways of those favored and those who go astray; the Community Rule develops a moral choice between the paths of truth and perversity, light and darkness.

column5: the straight path a person should choose
column6: The commentary asks God to lead a worshiping community on the straight way; this rabbinic teaching asks which straight path a person should choose and defines it by ethical conduct and its effects on others.

column5: the perilous afterlife path between fire and water
column6: The commentary explicitly corrects the popular image of ṣirāṭ as an afterlife bridge, saying the Qur'anic word is a road walked in this life; 4 Ezra pictures the narrow, dangerous path to the future city between fire and deep water.

column5: two ways, life and death
column6: The commentary names the straight way against the ways of anger and straying; the Didache opens its moral instruction by setting the way of life against the way of death.

column5: honest weights and balances
column6: The commentary hears mustaqīm's straightness as a scale that does not tip to either side; Leviticus commands honest weights and measures, making uprightness a practice of fair judgment.

column5: false balances are rejected
column6: The commentary links straightness with keeping the balance from leaning; Proverbs says dishonest scales are an abomination to the Lord, while a just weight pleases him.

column5: the scales belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary treats balance as part of the requested upright path; Proverbs says accurate scales and weights belong to the Lord, grounding fair measure in divine order.

column5: Arabic q-w-m; Hebrew q-w-m in “walk upright”
column6: The commentary labels al-mustaqīm with Arabic root q-w-m and develops upright bodily walking; Leviticus uses the cognate Hebrew root in saying God made Israel walk erect after breaking the yoke.

column5: Arabic q-w-m; Hebrew q-w-m, rise and stand
column6: The commentary labels al-mustaqīm with Arabic q-w-m and associates it with an upright walk; this verse uses the cognate Hebrew root for rising and standing upright, in contrast to enemies who fall.

column5: God upholds the falling and raises the bowed
column6: The commentary describes a traveler who sways and needs support before walking steadily; the psalm says God supports those who are falling and raises those bowed down.

column5: the Lord holds the hand of one who falls
column6: The commentary's route includes a dependent walker who needs support to continue; the psalm says even if the righteous person falls, the Lord holds his hand.

column5: humans cannot direct their own steps
column6: The commentary asks God to guide the collective because the traveler needs an outside guide; Jeremiah says a person's way is not in his own control and he cannot direct his steps.

column5: a way that seems right ends in death
column6: The commentary warns that a path's goodness depends on where it leads and who walks it; Proverbs warns that a way may seem right yet end in death.

column5: guide our feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary asks for guidance on a path that leads to a welcomed end; Zechariah's hymn says God's mercy will guide “our feet” into the way of peace, from darkness toward light.

column5: “lead us not into temptation”
column6: The commentary notes a communal “us” speaking directly to God in a pleading imperative; the Lord's Prayer likewise addresses God as “you” and asks collectively not to be led into trial but to be delivered from evil.

column5: belief that still asks for help
column6: The commentary says people already on the way still ask to be guided at every step; the father who says “I believe” immediately asks Jesus to help his unbelief.

column5: the shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow
column6: The commentary hears the guide as a leader who walks in front so others can follow; Jesus' shepherd calls his own sheep and goes ahead of them, and they follow.

column5: the Spirit guides into truth
column6: The commentary reserves guidance to God and connects the path with truth; Jesus says the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth.

column5: “unless someone guides me”
column6: The commentary describes a traveler unable to find the route alone; the Ethiopian reader asks how he can understand Isaiah unless someone guides him, and Philip joins him as an interpreter.

column5: the Christian movement called “the Way”
column6: The commentary stresses a path that is walked and followed, not a one-time threshold; Acts calls the community Saul seeks to arrest “the Way,” naming the movement as a lived route.

column5: the way that leads to life
column6: The commentary distinguishes the straight way from roads ending in loss; Jesus describes a narrow way leading to life, found by few, against the broad way leading to destruction.

column5: the Father's house as destination
column6: The commentary hears the road as leading to a home where the traveler is received; Jesus speaks of many dwelling places in his Father's house and going to prepare a place for his followers.

column5: Jesus as the way to the Father
column6: The commentary asks God to guide the collective on God's straight path; John identifies Jesus himself as the way through whom people come to the Father, giving the shared journey-to-God image a distinct Christian mediation.

column5: a new and living way into the sanctuary
column6: The commentary's path leads to a place of divine welcome; Hebrews describes access to the holy place through a new and living way opened through the veil, identified with Jesus' flesh.

column5: straight paths for the feet; healing the lame
column6: The commentary develops upright walking and the support needed by a wavering traveler; Hebrews applies the “straight paths” image to a community so the lame may be healed rather than disabled.

column5: abandoning the straight way
column6: The commentary says guidance must be sought again because a person can leave the path after finding it; Peter describes false teachers who have left the straight way and gone astray.

column5: grace as a gift, not earned payment
column6: The commentary says the requested guidance is a loving gift rather than a wage; Ephesians says salvation is by grace as God's gift, not the result of works.

column5: good works prepared for walking
column6: The commentary joins the gift of guidance to a path that must actually be walked; Ephesians says God prepared good works beforehand for people to walk in.

column5: the Lamb shepherds to springs of water
column6: The commentary combines a leading guide with the road's life-giving destination; Revelation says the Lamb will shepherd the multitude and guide them to springs of living water.

column5: following in the leader's steps
column6: The commentary pictures guidance as following an advance leader; Peter says Christ left an example so believers may follow in his steps.

column5: John applies Isaiah's straight-way prophecy to his own mission
column6: The commentary hears a requested path as the route along which a community must walk; John the Baptist identifies himself as the wilderness voice of Isaiah 40:3, interpreting preparation of the Lord's way as his prophetic task.
